sections.h2: What should a seller know about Lee County, Georgia property tax?
sections.html:
Lee County is the priciest of the four Georgia counties in the Census comparison, and its tax pages reflect a county that has grown fast. Leesburg is where both the tax commissioner and the tax assessors keep their offices, so most paperwork for a sale starts there.

The Census Bureau QuickFacts table puts the county at 34,179 people in mid-2025, up from 28,298 at the 2010 census. Land area is 355.88 square miles. Median value of an owner-occupied home is $231,800 for 2020 to 2024, 74.2 percent of homes are owner-occupied, and median household income is $89,168. Some 34.1 percent of adults hold a bachelor's degree or higher, and 65.5 percent of residents 16 and older are in the labor force.

Housing costs run higher here than in the neighboring counties on that list. Median gross rent is $1,184 and median owner costs with a mortgage are $1,605 a month. Builders pulled 94 permits in 2025. A buyer shopping in these numbers will ask what the annual tax runs, so have the latest bill and your exemption status in hand before you list.

sections.h2: Where are the Lee County tax commissioner and tax assessor offices?
sections.html:
Both are in Leesburg. The commissioner collects, the assessors value, and the Lee County tax site says plainly that the commissioner does not set values or millage rates.

The assessors' page says the three-member Board of Tax Assessors meets on the second Monday of each month at 4:30 p.m. at the Leslie Highway office, and it links to the online property records on qPublic. Lee County also provides a form for owners who want their records withheld from public listing.

The same page explains the setup: the county commissioners appoint the assessors to three year terms, and the assessors in turn appoint the chief appraiser. That chain matters if you want to raise a complaint about how the digest is run, since the board, not the tax commissioner, answers for values.

sections.h2: When are Lee County property taxes due?
sections.html:
Lee County property taxes are generally due by December 20, according to the county tax site. Bills mailed in to the Leesburg office are accepted on a United States Postal Service postmark, but a metered postmark does not count.

Interest and penalties follow the state rules in O.C.G.A. 48-2-40 and 48-2-44 once the due date passes, and the county warns that unpaid property may be levied upon and sold. Pay online at the tax commissioner's site if you want a record without a trip to Leesburg.

One quirk is specific to recent Lee County history. The tax site explains that refund checks for tax year 2025 went only to the owner of record on January 1, 2025, and not to mortgage or escrow companies. The commissioner's office does not prorate or split those checks between buyers and sellers:

  • A buyer who closed after January 1, 2025 should read the closing documents to see whether any share of the refund belongs to them.
  • Any division of the money is a private matter between buyer and seller.
  • Owners whose bill was paid through escrow can get a letter from the assessors' office to send to their mortgage servicer.

sections.h2: How are Lee County homes valued, and what is the appeal window?
sections.html:
You have 45 days from the date of the assessment notice to appeal. Appraisal staff set value from recent sales and market conditions as of January 1, and notices generally go out in the spring.

The county tax site describes the process in a few steps:

  • Assessed value is 40 percent of fair market value, unless another rate applies by law.
  • The written appeal goes first to the Board of Tax Assessors and must name the method you choose.
  • If you stay dissatisfied, the file moves to the county Board of Equalization, then Superior Court, or you may choose arbitration instead of the board.
  • The appeal cannot rest on a complaint about the amount of tax levied. Taxability, value and uniformity are the grounds.

Property tax returns go to the Board of Tax Assessors between January 1 and April 1, and real property returns renew themselves. Personal property returns are due every year. Standing timber is taxed only when it is sold or harvested, at 100 percent of fair market value, and a harvest report form is on the county site. For other questions about value, call 229-759-6010.

sections.h2: What homestead and other exemptions does Lee County offer?
sections.html:
Lee County has local exemptions on top of the state ones, and the local amount controls whenever it is larger than the state amount. The homestead application is filed with the Lee County Tax Assessor's Office, and April 1 is the deadline.

The county asks for a few specifics when you apply:

  • First-time homeowners should bring a copy of the warranty deed.
  • The driver's license must show the current Lee County physical address. A post office box is not accepted.
  • The exemption renews each year until you change residence or ownership or want a different kind of exemption.

The county tax page lists the standard $2,000 homestead exemption against the 40 percent assessed value, an elderly school tax exemption of up to $10,000 at age 62 when net income does not exceed $10,000, and an elderly general exemption of up to $4,000 at age 65. It also lists exemptions for disabled veterans and the surviving spouse of a firefighter or peace officer, a floating exemption at 62 with household income of $30,000 or less, and a deferral program at 62 with household income of $15,000 or less. Brownfield property can have its value frozen for ten years, and manufacturers may qualify for Freeport on inventory with an application between January 1 and April 1.

sections.h2: What happens to Lee County property tax when I sell?
sections.html:
The January 1 owner is responsible for the year's tax. Georgia gives no refund because someone sold part way through the year, per the Department of Revenue, so your closing attorney should divide the bill between buyer and seller.

Before you list, do these things:

  • Call the commissioner at 229-759-6015 and ask whether the current year is billed and paid.
  • Ask for a payoff if any balance remains.
  • Let the buyer know they must file their own homestead exemption, because yours does not transfer.

Census figures show 88.1 percent of Lee County residents lived in the same house a year earlier, so turnover is modest and a well-documented tax history is a selling point. If timber stood on your land, file the timber sale or harvest report that the county posts on both office pages, since the county taxes that timber when it is sold or cut.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Lee County property tax?
faqs.a: Pay the Lee County Tax Commissioner in Leesburg at 100 Starksville Avenue North, by mail to P.O. Box 9, or online through the county tax site.

faqs.q: Does a metered postmark count on a mailed Lee County payment?
faqs.a: No. The county accepts a United States Postal Service postmark, not a metered one, so mail early or pay online.

faqs.q: Who gets a Lee County refund check if the house sold?
faqs.a: The owner of record on January 1 of the tax year got the check. The commissioner does not split it, so buyer and seller settle it between themselves.

faqs.q: Do I need a deed to apply for a Lee County homestead exemption?
faqs.a: First-time homeowners should bring a copy of the warranty deed, along with a driver's license showing the Lee County physical address.

faqs.q: Can I appeal a Lee County value because my tax bill went up?
faqs.a: Not on that ground alone. An appeal must rest on taxability, value or uniformity, or on a denied exemption, and it must be filed within 45 days of the notice date.
